title: Quantum geometry and RKKY in flat bands
authors: Chang-geun Oh, Makoto Shimizu, Youichi Yanase, Shuichi Murakami
abstract: Flat conduction bands quench the group velocity and thus challenge conventional, dispersion-driven pictures of the Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida (RKKY) interaction, where localized moments are coupled via an effective exchange mediated by conduction electrons. Here we show that RKKY interactions in the flat-band limit are not extinguished by the vanishing group velocity but are instead mediated by the quantum geometry of Bloch states. Starting from a microscopic RKKY derivation, we demonstrate that the Brillouin-zone-averaged quantum metric controls the long-wavelength structure of the static susceptibility, thereby determining the magnetic correlation length and the spin stiffness. As a result, the finite spatial spread of Wannier functions provides an effective long-range coupling channel even when single-particle dispersion is absent. Furthermore, we establish the general principle that the ordering temperature is governed by the quantum metric in finite and low-dimensional samples, effectively circumventing the thermodynamic-limit constraint of the Mermin-Wagner theorem. Specifically, our theoretical investigation reveals that increasing the quantum metric enhances magnetic rigidity and leads to a corresponding rise in the critical temperature within finite-sized systems.
summary: This paper demonstrates that the RKKY interaction mediated by conduction electrons does not vanish in flat-band regimes; instead, it is governed by the quantum geometry of the Bloch states. The authors show this geometric coupling dictates magnetic rigidity and can stabilize finite-temperature magnetic order even in low dimensions. This establishes a general principle linking magnetism to the underlying electronic band structure's topology.
main_problem: The study investigates how the Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida (RKKY) interaction behaves when conduction electron bands are perfectly flat, challenging conventional pictures based on band dispersion.
main_result: RKKY interactions persist in the flat-band limit, mediated instead by the quantum geometry of Bloch states. This geometric coupling determines magnetic rigidity and can stabilize magnetic order in finite systems, circumventing Mermin-Wagner constraints.
method: The authors derive an effective RKKY Hamiltonian using microscopic derivations and analyze the long-wavelength structure of the static susceptibility ($\chi_0(\mathbf{q})$) via quantum geometry tensors.
model_or_system: The model involves localized magnetic moments coupled to conduction electrons on a lattice (e.g., 1D or 2D Lieb lattices). The analysis focuses on the flat-band limit and its extension to general itinerant systems by varying geometric parameters.
key_observables: RKKY interaction strength, static susceptibility $\chi_0(\mathbf{q})$, magnetic correlation length ($\xi$), and spin stiffness ($D$).
important_parameters: Quantum metric ($ ar{g}_{ab}$), bandwidth ($W$) to temperature ratio ($T$), and system size ($L$ or dimensionality $d$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on linear spin-wave theory approximations and assumes that the quantum metric provides a universal regulator for magnetic fluctuations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how varying geometric parameters (like $d_m$ or $\delta$) modulates the static susceptibility $\chi_0(q)$ in 1D/2D systems, showing changes from antiferromagnetic to ferromagnetic behavior and affecting critical temperature scaling with system size.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the failure of dispersion-driven RKKY in flat bands. It then introduces the quantum metric as the governing factor for long-range coupling. Finally, it generalizes this principle to finite and low-dimensional systems to explain magnetic stability beyond idealized limits.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful geometric mechanism (the quantum metric) to understand magnetic ordering in itinerant electron systems, offering insights applicable to materials where band structure engineering is key for spintronics or correlated magnetism.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic illustration of localized spins (red) interacting through a flat conduction band. The right panel depicts the band structure E(k) featuring a flat band (solid blue) at the Fermi level, separated from remote bands (dashed lines) by an energy gap ∆.

FIG. 2. Geometric stabilization of ferromagnetic order in a 1D RKKY model. (a) Energy dispersion of H1D c . The energy spectrum remains invariant under the tuning of the geometric parameter dm. (b) Static susceptibility χ0(q) for several values of dm = 0, 0.5 and 1. (c) Critical temperature Tc as a function of dm for fixed system sizes (L = 104, 105, 106). (d) Tc as a function of L for dm = 0.1, 0.5 and 1. Here, we fixed ∆= 0.3 for (b-c) and T = 0.01 for (b).

FIG. 3. Geometric stabilization of ferromagnetic order in a 2D RKKY model. (a) Energy dispersion of H2D c with δ = 0.4. (b) Determinant of the averaged quantum metric det ¯g as a function of δ. (c) Critical temperature Tc as a function of δ for fixed sys- tem sizes (L/a = 106, 1012, 1024). (d) Tc as a function of L for δ = 0.01, 0.05 and 0.1.

FIG. 4. Magnetic susceptibility in a 1D dispersive band. Static magnetic susceptibility χ0(q) as a function of momentum q for various quantum geometric parameters dm = {0, 0.7, 1.0}. (a) W/T = 40: Antiferromagnetic fluctuations dominate, with quantum geometry modulating the peak intensity. (b) W/T = 4: A transition from antiferromagnetic to ferromagnetic fluctuations occurs as dm increases. All calculations are performed at half-filling (µ = 0) with fixed parameters ∆= 0.3 and T = 0.01.

Magnetic noise spectroscopy.note: The paper calculates the static susceptibility $\chi_0(\mathbf{q})$ and discusses magnetic correlation length ($\xi$), which directly relates to the theoretical framework needed for modeling magnetic field noise from spin fluctuations via fluctuation-dissipation theorems.
